transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-08-29 16:00 PT | Duration: ~52m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (CTO - Synthrex), Renee Ortega (Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to map integration surface. Customer primarily API-first, using LangChain and an internal search index (homegrown) via LlamaIndex. Concerned about rate limits, VPC security, and observability hooks to attribute cost per feature.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex, AE for Redwood. Priya from our SE team is here. How's Synthrex?
[00:10] Jordan Miles: Hey Alex, doing good, thanks. We've got a few things to cover — mostly how we bolt Redwood into our existing pipeline. Renee and Samir are on for details.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Great — we usually like to walk through integration patterns first, then deployment options, and then ops concerns like quotas and observability. Sound ok?
[00:25] Renee Ortega: Yep. Quick context: our stack is Node + Python services, LangChain orchestrator, LlamaIndex for retrieval, and an internal gateway that all requests go through.
[00:34] Samir Patel: We run in a VPC, prefer private endpoints. Compliance team will want SOC2 artifacts and KMS integration.
[00:40] Alex Chen: Perfect. At a high level Redwood gives three modes — Hosted API for fastest time to value, Dedicated reserved capacity for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC / on-prem) for regulated workloads. We'll tailor integration examples for the one you choose.
[00:54] Jordan Miles: For us it's between Dedicated and Private. We might start with Dedicated for predictability but we need the option to move to Private later. Is that a common flow?
[01:02] Priya Nair: Very common. We support migrations — the application layer and SDK calls remain consistent. The main differences are network setup, data egress controls, and where the control plane lives.
[01:12] Renee Ortega: On SDKs — do you have a Python SDK idiomatic for LangChain? We already use the LangChain adapter but it's brittle across vendors.
[01:20] Priya Nair: Yes, we ship official SDKs in Python and Node. We also provide a LangChain integration example and a LlamaIndex adapter. I'll share a repo with a small wrapper that maps LangChain calls to Redwood streaming endpoints, including example for function-calling.
[01:33] Jordan Miles: Streaming is important for our UX. How does Redwood handle partial tokens and reconnection?
[01:38] Alex Chen: Streaming uses server-sent events or websockets depending on SDK. We manage rehydration of KV cache for resumed sessions; small chance of duplicate tokens on reconnect, but we provide idempotency keys on the request level.
[01:50] Samir Patel: About the gateway: we already have an internal API gateway that applies auth and routing. We prefer a proxy pattern where we call Redwood from a dedicated proxy service so we can centralize rate limits and retries. Thoughts?
[01:59] Priya Nair: That's a good pattern. Two approaches: 1) Sidecar/proxy per service that routes to Redwood with local caching for prefixes and a client-side rate limiter; or 2) centralized proxy that handles batching and per-customer quotas. Centralized is easier to enforce quotas but can be a single point of latency.
[02:18] Renee Ortega: We were thinking centralized for policy, but sidecars if latency gets tight. Can Redwood's SDKs do client-side batching?
[02:25] Priya Nair: SDKs support automatic batching for token generation and embedding calls — you can tune batch size and max latency. For LangChain we have a small middleware to coalesce requests. We can share config examples.
[02:36] Jordan Miles: How does billing and rate-limit enforcement interact? If we centralize, can we attribute token costs per feature flag or route?
[02:44] Alex Chen: Yes — Redwood's observability includes per-route and per-token cost breakdowns. You can attach metadata to requests (route, feature, user_id) and we surface cost and latency by those tags in Console. For Dedicated/Private you can still emit the same telemetry; the difference is retention and control plane access.
[02:58] Samir Patel: Network-wise for Private deployment, do we have to open outbound connections? Our security folks prefer inbound connections to a customer-controlled endpoint.
[03:06] Priya Nair: For on-prem Private, we can run the control plane in your VPC and the inference nodes can be placed in a private subnet. We support both outbound (from your VPC to Redwood-managed infra) and inbound (we deploy within customer infra). We'll map the exact topology in the network diagram I'll send.
[03:22] Renee Ortega: A few practical questions: 1) How do we integrate LlamaIndex so that retrieval augmented generation keeps our document scoring? 2) How do we cache embeddings?
[03:31] Priya Nair: For LlamaIndex we offer an adapter that converts index queries into embedding + retrieval calls. The pattern is to call Redwood embeddings endpoint for vectorization and then store vectors in your vector DB. For caching, we recommend local prefetch of embeddings for hot docs and use Redwood's prefix/KV cache for decoded prefix tokens to save generation tokens. Note that embeddings are charged per unit — we can show token math for expected QPS.
[03:54] Jordan Miles: Can that adapter run within our LangChain pipelines with minimal code changes?
[03:58] Priya Nair: Yes — the adapter is 10–20 lines to swap the embedding client. We'll provide a sample repo.
[04:05] Alex Chen: On quotas — you can set rate limits at key level, route level, and model variant level. For Dedicated we support guaranteed throughput with autoscale policies and burst windows. For Hosted there are quota guards to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[04:18] Samir Patel: We're worried about sudden spikes from agents — can we have circuit breakers that fallback to a smaller model?
[04:23] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Routing policies can fallback to cheaper compatible variants automatically. You can also set graceful degradation: lower max tokens, switch to quantized models, or route to cached responses.
[04:35] Renee Ortega: Observability — how granular are the traces? We want to correlate user request to token cost and model latency for our billing dashboard.
[04:43] Alex Chen: Console exposes trace ids you can propagate. We emit spans for request lifecycle, model token generation timeline, and batch processing. You can export traces to your tracing backend (Zipkin/Jaeger/OTel). There's also a token-level cost CSV export for accounting.
[04:58] Jordan Miles: About security — KMS/HSM support? SAML SSO for Console?
[05:03] Priya Nair: Yes to both. Private and Dedicated tiers support customer-managed KMS integrations and HSM for key isolation. We support SAML/SSO and role-based access controls; audit logs are available for enterprise retention settings.
[05:14] Samir Patel: Any gotchas with our current gateway doing TLS termination then calling Redwood?
[05:18] Alex Chen: If your gateway terminates TLS, ensure you use mTLS between gateway and the Redwood SDK endpoint or enable signed JWTs. We recommend mTLS for Private deployments.
[05:28] Renee Ortega: Latency — we need p99 end-to-end under 350ms for short prompts. What's realistic?
[05:34] Priya Nair: For short prompts on Dedicated with local region GPUs, typical p99 is 80–200ms depending on model size and batch patterns. On-prem can be similar if you deploy near your traffic and use our optimized runtime. We'll run an on-prem PoC to validate with your dataset — that will be the best data point.
[05:51] Jordan Miles: For the PoC, can we stream live traffic or use replay?
[05:55] Alex Chen: Both. Many customers do replay to validate correctness, then a shadow traffic run to validate latency and quotas. We'll provide the tooling and a checklist to avoid exposing PII in the test.
[06:06] Renee Ortega: About SDK errors and retries: what's the recommended retry/backoff? We currently implement exponential backoff with jitter at the gateway level.
[06:14] Priya Nair: That pattern is fine. SDKs have built-in retry hooks, idempotency tokens, and retryable error classification. For rate-limit responses we return standard HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. For batched requests, partial failures include per-item status which the client can handle.
[06:31] Samir Patel: Any limitations with LlamaIndex regarding tokenization differences across models? We use a mix of Open models; tokenization variance affects chunking logic.
[06:40] Priya Nair: Tokenization can vary by model family. In the adapter we surface a tokenizer module that normalizes chunking heuristics and we recommend running a small tokenization calibration script against your corpus. We'll include that in the repo.
[06:55] Jordan Miles: What about cost control — can we set hard caps per env?
[06:59] Alex Chen: Yes, hard caps per API key, route, or customer; soft alerts precede hard caps. Console can also auto-disable routes when spend exceeds threshold.
[07:08] Renee Ortega: Any prebuilt dashboards for monitoring embedding usage vs generative?
[07:12] Priya Nair: Console has templates: embeddings, generations, latency, and per-route cost. We can also provide CSV/JSON exports for internal billing pipelines.
[07:20] Jordan Miles: Great. Any examples of customers doing the sidecar + central policy approach?
[07:24] Alex Chen: Yes — a couple of mid-market analytics customers do that: local sidecars for latency at the service boundary + central proxy for quota accounting. We'll anonymize and share patterns.
[07:35] Renee Ortega: Ok that's helpful. For our immediate next steps: security pack, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter, sample SDKs, and schedule PoC.
[07:43] Alex Chen: Sounds good. Priya, can you take point on the sample repos and the PoC runbook?
[07:48] Priya Nair: Yep — I'll drop the LangChain adapter, LlamaIndex example, and a small proxy sample with rate-limit snippets. Expect links in 48 hours.
[07:57] Jordan Miles: Perfect. We'll pull together the dataset and confirm the PoC scope by next week. Renee will coordinate.
[08:03] Renee Ortega: Thanks everyone. One last thing — do you have a quick blurb on model variants and quantization? We might need smaller cheaper models for high-volume agents.
[08:10] Priya Nair: Short answer: we support quantized variants for many families; routing policies can swap variants automatically when cost thresholds hit. We'll include a model recommendation doc tuned to your workload.
[08:20] Alex Chen: Closing recap — we'll send security docs, share SDK and adapter repos, and schedule an on-prem latency PoC. Any blockers?
[08:27] Jordan Miles: None for now. Thanks!
[08:30] Alex Chen: Thanks all — talk soon.

Action items (recap): Alex: security materials + pricing; Priya: repos and PoC runbook; Renee: dataset and token volumes; schedule PoC week-of 2027-09-13.

Notes: Small transcription artifacts: "K V cash" appeared once instead of KV cache; LangChain sometimes transcribed as "Lang Chain". Some speaker labels merged briefly when crosstalk occurred.
